paper_title: UltraTex: Aligning Physical Knowledge for High-Fidelity PBR Texture Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. While current generative methods produce realistic albedo maps, they still struggle to infer accurate metallic and roughness attributes for relighting. We present UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi-view diffusion-based PBR generation. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albedo maps, and then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference image, and material semantic priors. To inject material semantics, a lightweight adapter transforms hidden-layer features of a vision-language model (VLM) into intrinsic material representation tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. To model material-light interaction, photometric representation alignment guides intermediate diffusion features toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting. This makes metallic and roughness variations observable through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance for fine-grained material prediction without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments show that UltraTex generates high-quality textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Physically based rendering (PBR) is the industry standard for material representation of 3D assets in games, films, and AR/VR [Burley 2012; Pharr et al. 2016]. PBR texture maps separate visible appearance from intrinsic material attributes, enabling assets to respond plausibly under different lighting conditions. While albedo defines the base color of surface, realistic relighting depends critically on properties such as metallic and roughness. These attributes describe physical reflectance behavior rather than directly observable image signals, making high-quality PBR texture authoring labor-intensive process that still relies heavily on expert-driven workflows [Adobe Systems Inc. 2024]. Generating PBR texture maps for 3D mesh from single reference image is therefore highly ambiguous. The observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, geometry, and illumination. For example, bright region in the input may arise from polished metal, glossy dielectric coating, baked illumination, or local color pattern. This ambiguity is especially severe for metallic roughness (MR) estimation, where the desired outputs are abstract intrinsic maps rather than natural RGB images. Early inverse-rendering methods reduce this ambiguity by using controlled capture setups, such as co-located flash lighting, to expose physical cues like specular highlights [Bao et al. 2025; Guo et al. 2021; Ma et al. 2021]. Although effective in constrained environments, these methods do not generalize well to arbitrary in-the-wild images. Recent generative approaches instead leverage powerful image-domain priors from diffusion models [BlackForestLabs 2024; Esser et al. 2024; Rombach et al. 2022] and multi-view generation techniques [Huang et al. 2024a; Seed3D 2026; Shi et al. 2023; Team 2025a] to synthesize multi-view texture or PBR images, which are then reprojected onto the mesh surface to construct texture maps. While this paradigm has substantially improved albedo generation, it remains unreliable for intrinsic MR prediction. Existing methods often assign metallic values to incorrect regions or produce overly conservative roughness maps with limited fine-scale variation. These failures indicate that strong appearance priors alone are insufficient: the model must also understand what each object part is made of and how its material should respond to light. Professional PBR creation follows this reasoning naturally: artists infer material maps by considering asset style, part-wise material composition, surface structure, and illumination behavior, rather 2 than matching pixels alone. We argue that high-fidelity PBR generation requires aligning such physical knowledge with the generative process. This alignment can be achieved in two complementary ways. First, physical knowledge can be injected as conditioning priors for material semantics. Vision-language models are well suited for this role, as their hidden representations encode rich world knowledge and semantic reasoning from large-scale image-text pretraining; however, an adapter is needed to translate them into diffusion-compatible material tokens. Second, physical knowledge can guide learning through training objectives. Since metallic and roughness maps are abstract intrinsic parameters whose effects become visible only after interacting with albedo, geometry, and illumination, MR generation should be supervised in photometric representation space where controlled-light renderings reveal material-light responses. To this end, we introduce UltraTex, cascaded multi-view framework for high-quality PBR texture generation from single reference image and an input mesh. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to obtain detailed albedo maps, and then predicts MR maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference-image features, and material semantic priors. For materialsemantic conditioning, we introduce VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter that transforms hidden-layer vision-language features into intrinsic material tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. For photometric guidance, we propose photometric representation alignment, which guides intermediate MR diffusion features toward visual representations of ground-truth materials rendered under controlled lighting. This rendered RGB space reveals fine-grained MR variations through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraTex generates highquality PBR textures and substantially outperforms state-of-the-art open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility. In summary, we make the following contributions: To the best of our knowledge, we present the first diffusionbased PBR texture generation framework that explicitly aligns physical knowledge through material-semantic conditioning and photometric representation guidance. We introduce VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter that translates hidden-layer vision-language features into material-aware tokens, injecting part-wise semantic priors into MR generation. We propose photometric representation alignment, which guides intermediate MR diffusion features with controlled-light material renderings to capture fine-grained material-light interactions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraTex substantially outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
2.1 Texture Generation
sections.content: Foundation models have opened new directions for automating texture generation in 3D content creation. Early methods adopt optimization-based paradigms, using Score Distillation Sampling

sections.title: 2.2 PBR Texture Generation
sections.content: Building upon texture synthesis, recent methods extend pretrained diffusion models to PBR material generation. Early works incorporate BRDF formulations into SDS optimization to infer material properties [Chen et al. 2023a; Liu et al. 2024a; Wu et al. 2023; Xu et al. 2023; Yeh et al. 2024; Youwang et al. 2024a; Zhang et al. 2024a], but often struggle to decompose lighting and surface reflectance, leading to unrealistic or flat results. To enhance spatial alignment and material accuracy, subsequent approaches either employ iterative latent synchronization [Huang et al. 2024b; Zhang et al. 2024c] or leverage LLMs for retrievalaugmented generation [Dang et al. 2024; Fang et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024; Wei et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2024b]. Despite this, these methods primarily transfer generative priors to the PBR task without endto-end training on large-scale PBR datasets, which fundamentally constrains their generalization ability. recent line of work fine-tunes image or video models to predict multi-channel PBR maps [Hasselgren et al. 2026; He et al. 2025; Ma et al. 2025; Munkberg et al. 2025; Vainer et al. 2024; Vecchio et al. 2024; Yuan et al. 2025; Zhu et al. 2024]. These methods mainly transfer appearance-generation priors to intrinsic material prediction through pixel-level reconstruction losses. While scalable, this transfer does not directly resolve the ambiguity of MR estimation, where metallic and roughness are latent material properties rather than observable appearance. As result, these models remain biased toward appearance matching, leading to frequent ambiguity in intrinsic material decomposition. In contrast, our method introduces explicit material reasoning from VLM world knowledge and representation-level photometric regularization to provide semantic and physical supervision for MR generation.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Given single reference image and an input mesh, UltraTex generates cross-view consistent PBR texture maps through cascaded two-stage multi-view diffusion pipeline  (Fig. 2)  . Stage 1 jointly predicts orthographic-view albedo maps and world-space shading normals from the reference image and multi-view geometry normals (Sec. 3.1). Conditioned on the generated albedo, Stage 2 predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps with VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter (Sec. 3.2.1) and photometric representation alignment (Sec. 3.2.2). Both stages are built upon an image diffusion backbone and are trained separately; following [Team 2025a], MR maps are represented as two channels of single RGB image.

sections.title: 3.1 Multi-view Albedo and Shading Normal Generation
sections.content: The first stage generates multi-view albedo maps and world-space shading normals from the reference image and rendered geometry normals. We adopt two-step architecture: Multi-Modal Transformer (MM-T) fuses conditioning tokens and noisy view latents per view, then Multi-View Transformer (MV-T) models cross-view interactions for global consistency. 3.1.1 Multi-Modal DiT. For each view, MM-T integrates the reference-image and geometry-normal conditions into unified latent representation. Specifically, for the 𝑖-th view, we extract geometrynormal tokens T𝑖 geo by encoding the rendered geometry normal 𝑮𝑖 Fig. 2. Overall pipeline of UltraTex. UltraTex adopts cascaded two-stage multi-view diffusion pipeline. Stage 1 jointly predicts albedo maps and worldspace shading normals from the reference image and multi-view geometry normals. Stage 2 predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps (where purple and green represent roughness and metallic, respectively) conditioned on the generated albedo, reference-image features, and VLM-derived intrinsic material tokens. For MR training, photometric representation alignment uses frozen visual encoder to extract representations from controlled-light material renderings, and an MLP aligns intermediate diffusion features to this photometric representation space via LREPA. (SDS) [Poole et al. 2023] to distill priors from pretrained 2D diffusion models into 3D assets [Chen et al. 2023b, 2022; Khalid et al. 2022; Lin et al. 2023; Metzer et al. 2022; Michel et al. 2021; Po and Wetzstein 2024; Poole et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2023]. However, iterative optimization over renderings is costly and often produces over-saturated textures or artifacts that limit practical use. Feed-forward approaches explored progressive inpainting across pre-defined views conditioned on explicit 3D attributes [Bensadoun et al. 2024; Cao et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2024b; Yu et al. 2023]. However, the geometric fidelity is frequently compromised by the cross-view latent synchronization. Alternatively, to bypass such occlusion and alignment issues, other methods directly target the UV space [Bensadoun et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2023, 2024; Zeng et al. 2024]. Yet, the topological fragmentation inherent to UV parameterizations severely degrades the generative capacity of 2D diffusion models, hindering high-fidelity synthesis. Recent methods [He et al. 2026; Huang et al. 2024a; Liu et al. 2025; Yeo et al. 2026; Zhao et al. 2025] incorporate multi-view attention mechanisms [Feng et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2024c; Kant et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024; Shi et al. 2023; Wang and Shi 2023] to generate globally consistent textures while respecting 3D geometry. However, they mainly target appearance texturing, producing either albedo maps or illumination-baked textures without intrinsic material attributes required for physically based relighting. Another line of work performs texture generation directly in native 3D space [Chen et al. 2026; Lai et al. 2025; Xiang et al. 2025; Zeng et al. 2025]. These methods directly generate complete surface textures in 3D space, providing inherent geometric consistency while avoiding view-projection artifacts such as edge bleeding. sections.title: 3.2 Multi-view MR Generation
sections.content: Our multi-view MR generator follows the same MM-T/MV-T architecture as the albedo model in Sec. 3.1, but replaces the geometrynormal condition with the Stage-1 albedo maps. It further introduces two physical knowledge alignment modules for intrinsic material estimation: VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter and photometric representation alignment. 3.2.1 VLM-Guided Intrinsic Material Adapter. Before training the multi-view MR generator, we train VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter in separate stage, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The goal is to translate material-aware visual knowledge from frozen visionlanguage model (VLM) into diffusion-compatible intrinsic material tokens. During this adapter training stage, both the VLM and the image diffusion model are kept frozen, and only the adapter is optimized. Previous studies [Kaduri et al. 2025; Neo et al. 2024] indicate that VLM hidden representations evolve progressively across layers: early layers capture raw visual features, whereas intermediate layers encode more abstract semantic and reasoning cues. Since MR generation requires reasoning about intrinsic material properties rather than direct appearance transfer, we exploit intermediate VLM tokens extracted from the encoded reference image 𝑰 as source of material-aware context. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: These tokens are injected into the frozen image diffusion model through token-wise concatenation in the denoising blocks, where they interact with noisy latents to reconstruct ground-truth metallic and roughness maps. We optimize the adapter with the standard flow-matching objective on rendered reference images paired with their ground-truth MR maps. After training, the learned tokens encode part-aware material semantic priors and are used as conditional inputs for Stage-2 MR generation. 3.2.2 Photometric Representation Alignment. Inspired by representation alignment methods such as REPA [Yu et al. 2025], we introduce photometric representation alignment to provide stronger guidance for MR generation. Directly aligning raw MR maps with pretrained visual encoders is ill-posed, since encoders such as DINOv2 [Oquab et al. 2023] and MAE [He et al. 2022] are trained on natural images, while metallic and roughness maps are abstract intrinsic parameters. To bridge this domain gap, we construct alignment targets in photometrically meaningful RGB space. For each training view, we render the ground-truth materials into an auxiliary photometric response xpm under controlled point-light setup, where the light source is collocated with the camera. The rendered response exposes material-light interactions, such as highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, while remaining compatible with pretrained visual encoders. We use frozen DINOv2 encoder 𝑓 to extract the target representation = 𝑓 (xpm). During MR generation, the intermediate transformer features h𝑡 at timestep 𝑡 are projected by MLP layer ℎ𝜙 and aligned with y: LREPA (𝜃, 𝜙) = E(x,xpm ),𝑡 1 𝑁𝑝 𝑁𝑝 𝑛=1 (cid:16) y𝑛, ℎ𝜙 (h[𝑛] 𝑡 ) sim (cid:17) , (11) where 𝑁𝑝 denotes the number of patches and sim(, ) is the patchwise cosine similarity. sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: 4.1.1 Dataset. We curate dataset of 130K objects from ObjaverseXL [Deitke et al. 2023a,b] and TexVerse [Zhang et al. 2025]. For diversity, each object is rendered into 32 reference images under random cameras and environment maps. For supervision, we extract ground-truth PBR maps (albedo, metallic, roughness), normals (geometry, shading), and render photometric images across six 10242 orthogonal views. We provide more details in the supplementary. 4.1.2 Training. We use the intrinsic material token adapter to integrate the Qwen3.5-4B VLM [Qwen Team 2026] with our diffusion framework. The adapter is two-layer MLP with channel dimensions {12288, 4096, 3072} and an intermediate SiLU activation. Hierarchical visual features are extracted from intermediate VLM layers = {8, 16, 24}. Both the albedo and MR models initialize their DiT backbones from pretrained text-to-image diffusion model. The multi-view models are trained at per-view resolution of 7682. Each model is trained on 32 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for about 2 days. Inference. At inference time, we first generate six-view albedo 4.1.3 maps, which then condition the MR network to estimate corresponding metallic and roughness maps. All maps per view are upscaled to 15362 by super-resolution module and mapped onto 4K UV textures. To ensure complete surface coverage, unobserved regions not captured by the orthogonal projections are inpainted using the novel view synthesis model from LumiTex [Bao et al. 2026] (see original paper for details).

To evaluate texture fidelity, we follow the protocol of Hunyuan3D [Team 2025a,b; Zhao et al. 2025] by employing FID [Heusel et al. 2017], CLIP-FID, and LPIPS [Zhang et al. 2018]. For more fine-grained assessment, we use CLIP Maximum-Mean Discrepancy (CMMD) [Jayasumana et al. 2024] to measure detail diversity and CLIP-I [Radford et al. 2021] for prompt alignment. Notably, all aforementioned perceptual and semantic metrics are computed exclusively on the albedo maps. For MR estimation, accuracy is validated via the MSE (103). We also conduct user study to benchmark texture quality based on human preferences. 4.2.3 Quantitative Results. We quantitatively compare UltraTex with baselines on 152 held-out Objaverse-XL objects, using Blenderrendered GT assets as reference inputs and rendering outputs at 10242 resolution. Except for MSE on MR attributes, all perceptual and semantic metrics are computed on rendered albedo/MR images, covering visual fidelity, semantic alignment, and PBR accuracy. 6 As shown in Tab. 1, our method consistently outperforms existing baselines across all metrics. It achieves better FID and LPIPS for perceptual quality, lower CMMD for texture diversity, higher CLIPI/CLIP-FID for semantic alignment, and the lowest MSE across PBR attributes, validating its superior physical accuracy. Additionally, Table 3 further shows that our method outperforms both the stateof-the-art multi-view baseline (LumiTex) and the 3D-native baseline (TRELLIS.2) under environment relighting. To evaluate perceptual quality, we conduct blind user study where 31 professional 3D modelers rate results from 1 to 5 based on overall rendering, albedo, roughness, and metallic fidelity. UltraTex achieves the highest scores across all dimensions (Tab. 2) and substantially outperforms competitors in pairwise win rates  (Fig. 5)  , demonstrating strong expert preference. 4.2.4 Qualitative Results. We qualitatively compare UltraTex with recent open-source and commercial baselines for PBR texture generation. For test data, we generate reference images via Seedream 4.5 [Seedream et al. 2025], followed by mesh generation with Hunyuan3D v3.1, then apply each method for texture generation. As shown in Fig. 6 and 7, existing methods like Hunyuan3D and Hyper3D often suffer from illumination leakage, producing albedo maps with baked-in lighting artifacts. Furthermore, most baselines have difficulty resolving intrinsic material ambiguity, frequently misclassifying metallic regions or producing over-smoothed roughness maps. In contrast, by leveraging material knowledge and illumination cues, UltraTex consistently produces more accurate metallic estimates and fine-grained roughness details, while also delivering albedo maps with superior physical fidelity and structural richness. This advantage is especially evident in challenging cases  (Fig. 8)  , including micro-scale roughness variations, oxidized or coated metals, and part-wise material changes, where baselines often fail. Furthermore, the diverse gallery in Fig. 18 demonstrates our models ability to produce physically plausible textures across wide array of geometric complexities and material compositions. We further evaluate the generated PBR textures through relighting under diverse novel illumination conditions. As shown in Fig. 9, the recovered material properties respond naturally to changes in lighting, producing consistent highlights, reflections, and surface appearance across different environments. To further evaluate the accuracy of intrinsic material decomposition, we compare against baselines on objects with ground-truth PBR maps. Given the same clay mesh and reference image, UltraTex more faithfully recovers the target material properties than the multi-view baseline LumiTex and the 3D-native baseline TRELLIS.2, particularly in base color, metallic separation, and spatially varying roughness  (Fig. 11)  . 4.2.5 Results on Real-World Inputs. We further evaluate UltraTex on casually captured real-world inputs and scanned meshes, including three examples collected from Sketchfab and two from the DTC dataset [Dong et al. 2025]. These inputs exhibit uncontrolled illumination, appearance ambiguity, and imperfect scanned geometry. As shown in Fig. 10, UltraTex remains robust under these conditions, producing coherent PBR materials and physically plausible relighting. The results demonstrate that our method generalizes beyond clean rendered inputs to practical real-world asset creation. Fig. 6. Comparison with open source methods. Our method effectively eliminates baked-in lighting and shadows, ensuring the generation of physically accurate material attributes. We show the albedo channel (left) alongside the metallic (top right) and roughness (bottom right) channels. Fig. 7. Comparison with SoTA commercial methods. Recent commercial methods often struggle with accurate metallic and roughness estimation. By integrating VLM-based physical reasoning and photometric consistency, UltraTex generates more accurate material attributes and richer material details. For each asset, we show the albedo channel (left) alongside the metallic (top right) and roughness (bottom right) channels.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.content: VLM-derived Intrinsic Material Token. To validate the impact of VLM priors, we train variant of MR estimation network without intrinsic material token guidance. As shown in Fig. 12 and Tab. 4, removing the VLM-derived tokens leads to clear material misclassification and increases both metallic and roughness errors. The ablated model relies heavily on low-level visual cues, such as color and specular highlights, and therefore mistakes strong reflections for metallic materials. This confirms that VLM guidance provides essential semantic and part-level material priors, enabling more physically grounded MR estimation that is robust to misleading appearance-based heuristics. In addition, removing the visual conditions also degrades MR quality, demonstrating their complementary role in providing dense spatial guidance for material generation. Decoding Probe of VLM Encoder. To quantify the intrinsic material information encoded by the 1D material tokens, we conduct decoding probe by replacing the VLM encoder with VAE and DINOv2 encoders under the same setting and directly decoding MR maps from the resulting tokens. As shown in Tab. 5, VLM features consistently outperform VAE and DINOv2 features, demonstrating that the resulting tokens carry richer material semantics and better disentangle intrinsic MR properties from observed appearance. This is because intrinsic material properties require semantic reasoning beyond observable appearance, which is better captured by the world knowledge encoded in VLM representations. VLM-token Attention Map Visualization. To better understand the part-level spatial localization of the 1D material tokens, we visualize the attention from VLM tokens to noisy image tokens at the 4th layer of the Multi-Modal DiT. As shown in Fig. 13, the responses 7 Fig. 8. Comparison of local details. Our model excels in generating ultrafine albedo details with high fidelity, even for challenging surfaces such as oxidized metals and those characterized by intricate micro-textures. Fig. 9. Our generated PBR textures exhibit physically plausible and consistent material responses under novel illumination conditions, faithfully reflecting changes in highlights and reflections. Table 4. Notably, the VLM tokens themselves carry no explicit spatial coordinates; their spatial correspondence emerges through interaction with the image tokens inside the DiT. This indicates that the material tokens are not merely used as global semantic conditions, but establish part-level correspondence with regions exhibiting the associated material properties. Photometric Regularization Loss. To investigate the role of representation level photometric alignment, we compare our full model against variant trained without this mechanism. As shown in Fig. 12, removing this constraint causes the model to regress toward 8 Fig. 10. Results on real-world captures. This degradation is especially prominent in roughness estimation, where high-frequency variations on materials such as painted metal, wood, and stone are suppressed. These results demonstrate that intrinsic reflectance properties cannot be robustly inferred from semantic priors alone; the model requires explicit cues regarding surface response to illumination. Photometric alignment supplies essential, complementary reflectance information for physically accurate MR estimation. Joint Shading Normal Estimation. To evaluate the impact of our joint prediction strategy, we compare our model against baseline trained solely on albedo. As shown in Fig. 4, omitting joint shading-normal estimation leads to visibly smoother albedo maps and weaker surface structures, especially around fine engravings and material boundaries. This confirms that joint generation is essential for preserving rich, high-frequency surface details, and significantly enhances the visual realism of the final renderings through these enriched surface bump. Fig. 11. Qualitative comparison with ground-truth PBR maps. Given the same clay mesh and reference image, our method more faithfully recovers the ground-truth material decomposition than the state-of-the-art multi-view and 3D-native baselines, with finer base-color details, cleaner metallic separation, and more accurate spatially varying roughness. Without VLM-derived tokens, the network incorrectly predicts non-metallic surfaces (e.g., painted fish, plastic TV casing) as metallic. Removing photometric alignment yields weaker metallic contrast and fails to recover structural details like gears, rivets, and screws. VAE Reconstruction Quality. This issue is also relevant to our framework, as we exploit an image-model prior and encode metallicroughness (MR) maps with an RGB-pretrained VAE. We therefore compute standard VAE reconstruction metrics on 366 MR view maps by comparing the original and reconstructed MR maps. The attention maps exhibit clear spatial localization over material-relevant object parts, such as metallic ornaments and hardware, indicating that the 1D material tokens capture part-aware material correspondence. for PBR material maps, our evaluation shows that it retains the key material information with minimal reconstruction distortion, supporting its use for MR generation in our framework.

sections.title: 4.4 Applications
sections.content: Multi-view Input Extension. Multi-view references are common in practical content-creation workflows, as they provide complementary observations of object appearance and reduce ambiguity in occluded regions and material properties. As illustrated in Fig. 14, 9 Fig. 14. Multi-view input pipeline. Our framework naturally extends to multi-view references by independently encoding each input view and pairing its image features with the corresponding geometry tokens in the MultiModal DiT, while leaving the remaining generation pipeline unchanged. Fig. 15. Normal map transformation. Our predicted shading normals are converted to tangent-space normal map, adding fine-scale surface details to the original clay mesh without modifying its geometry. our framework can be naturally extended to support multi-view inputs with only minor modification to the Multi-Modal DiT, while leaving the remaining generation pipeline unchanged. Specifically, given set of reference images {𝑰𝑖 }𝑁 𝑖=1, we construct an image token for each view by replacing Eq. 2 with 𝑖 img = Linearimg [EVAE (𝑰𝑖 ); DINOv2(𝑰𝑖 )] , where each reference view is independently encoded into its corresponding appearance representation. We then pair the image token with the geometry token of the same view and perform multi-modal fusion as (15) 𝑙1 𝑙1 𝑖 = MM-T 𝒛 (cid:16) 𝑖 𝒛𝑖, img 𝑖 , geo (cid:17) . (16) This view-wise formulation preserves the original architecture and enables the model to incorporate complementary appearances from multiple observations with minimal changes to the original pipeline. Normal Map Transformation. Our predicted shading normals can be directly converted into standard tangent-space normal map using the local surface frame of the mesh. As shown in Fig. 15, applying the resulting normal map to the original clay mesh enriches its shading with fine-scale surface details without modifying the Fig. 16. Failure Cases. Highly stylized assets may use MR for artistic rather than physical effects, leading to ambiguous decomposition, as seen in the jokers hair and the characters garments. In addition, effects beyond the opaque metallicroughness model, such as the vehicles transparent windshield, cannot be faithfully represented. underlying geometry. In particular, subtle structures such as the helmet engravings, facial details, and hair strands become substantially more pronounced, producing more detailed and realistic surface appearance.

sections.title: 4.5 Failure Cases
sections.content: Our main failure mode arises on highly stylized UGC assets, where PBR attributes are often manipulated to achieve desired artistic appearance rather than to faithfully represent physical material properties. In particular, metallic may serve as an appearance control for highlights, contrast, or stylized reflectance, making the decomposition fundamentally ambiguous from appearance alone. As shown in Fig. 16, the jokers hair and the characters garments exhibit simultaneously high metallic and roughness valuesan artistically plausible choice that does not correspond to their physical material identity. Our predictions may therefore remain visually and physically plausible while differing from such intentionally nonphysical reference values. separate limitation arises from material effects beyond our current PBR parameterization: for example, the transparent windshield of the stylized vehicle in Fig. 16 cannot be faithfully represented by the opaque metallicroughness model.

sections.title: 5 Conclusions
sections.content: We presented UltraTex, cascaded multi-view framework for singleimage PBR texture generation that moves beyond appearance matching by aligning physical knowledge with diffusion-based material generation. By integrating VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter for part-wise semantic priors and photometric representation alignment for material-light interaction, UltraTex generates high-fidelity metallic and roughness maps with improved physical plausibility and relighting behavior. In addition, joint estimation of world-space shading normals with albedo provides geometry-aware supervision, Fig. 17. More Qualitative Results. We present additional PBR comparisons with other methods (from left to right: albedo, metallic, roughness). Zooming in for details. 11 Fig. 18. More results. We provide additional multi-view renderings with their corresponding generated PBR maps. Zooming in is recommended to observe the ultra-fine albedo and material details. 12 enriching surface detail and improving albedo fidelity. Comprehensive evaluations on diverse assets demonstrate that UltraTex substantially outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility, highlighting its potential for high-quality 3D asset creation. Limitations and Future Work. Despite its strong generative capability, UltraTex still faces challenges with complex materials involving non-standard light transport. For example, as shown in Fig. 18, the model may approximate gemstones using albedo patterns and low roughness values, but cannot faithfully represent transparency, translucency, caustics, or more detailed BRDF effects. This limitation stems partly from the restricted material channels used in current training data, which focus on albedo, metallic, and roughness. promising direction is to incorporate additional material channels, such as specular, coat, transmission, and subsurface scattering, once sufficiently large-scale datasets with such annotations become available. Another direction is to extend the framework toward more expressive material models while preserving the robustness and scalability of multi-view PBR generation.
